examples: Even though I got covered in mud, I ran all the way to the end.
He changed out of his sweat-soaked shirt.
Please do not touch it with blood-covered hands.
A report riddled with lies will lose people's trust.
I want to escape from a life buried in debt.
Carefully wipe down the oil-covered machine.
fields.explain:
Preferably used with substances that “stick/spread/run”; in metaphorical use, it carries a strongly negative implication.
In polite speech or journalistic description, まみれ creates a vivid, sometimes heavy impression.
Not used with positive/lovely things (×花まみれ → use花だらけ/花いっぱい).

• “Full of / smeared with / covered in N”, usually dirt or something unpleasant (泥, 砂, 血, 汗, 油, ほこり...).
• Can be used metaphorically for a state of being steeped in something negative: 嘘まみれ, 噂まみれ, 借金まみれ.
• Difference from だらけ: まみれ emphasizes “covering the surface/the whole body”; だらけ emphasizes “many mistakes/flaws scattered about”.
fields.notes:
• The image of “まみれる” suggests unpleasantness/dirtiness → metaphorical use creates a strong nuance of criticism.
• With absorbent things (紙, 布), it describes being soaked: 血まみれ/汗まみれ sounds stronger than 濡れた.
• Can be combined with adjectives: 汗まみれで臭う (covered in sweat and smelly).
mistakes: Using it with positive nouns → unnatural: × 褒め言葉まみれ → use 褒め言葉だらけ instead.
Using it for “mistakes/errors” → choose ～だらけ: × 間違いまみれ → ◯ 間違いだらけ.
Forgetting the negative nuance → the sentence sounds too heavy in a light context.

rows: Emphasizes the surface/being stuck on; negative
<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>いだらけの<ruby>作文<rt>さくぶん</rt></ruby>
<ruby>白<rt>しろ</rt></ruby>づくめの<ruby>服装<rt>ふくそう</rt></ruby>

fields.meaning: … goes without saying, but … even more
examples: His singing ability is impressive, of course, but his expressiveness is truly overwhelming.
The location is one thing, but it is the excellent after-sales service that has earned it a good reputation.
Its speed is impressive, but it outperforms other companies even more in stability.
The design is great, but the functionality is truly outstanding.
Experience matters, but we place even greater value on a strong sense of ethics.
The scale of the damage is serious enough, but the impact of harmful rumors is even more serious.
fields.explain:
Used in praise/professional evaluations, PR texts, and presentations.
N1 and the following part should be on the same axis of evaluation (quality, service, people...).
Difference from “だけでなく”: it emphasizes the move of raising A and then pushing B forward as “even more”.

• “Not only is A significant, but B is even more so.” A is raised first, then the focus shifts to B.
• Polite nuance; used in advertising/introductions/formal evaluations; usually positive, but can also be used with negatives.
• The following part is the informational focus; avoid putting important content in A.
fields.notes:
• Has a refined, literary quality; in copywriting it makes the sentence sound more “classy”.
• Often paired with contrasting/supporting words: まして／なおさら／とりわけ in part B to add emphasis.
• It is fine to set more than one criterion as A, but take care not to blur the focus on B.
mistakes: Placing a verb/adjective directly before it → unnatural; use nominalization if needed.
Putting important information in A → loses its effect; B is the focus to be emphasized.
Confusing it with ～はおろか (negative) or ～だけでなく (neutral) → wrong nuance on the exam.

rows: Not only A, B even more
Formal; B is the focus; elevating nuance
<ruby>外見<rt>がいけん</rt></ruby>もさることながら、<ruby>中身<rt>なかみ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby>
A goes without saying, B too
Neutral; not necessarily “B more than A”
<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>はもちろん、<ruby>価格<rt>かかく</rt></ruby>も<ruby>魅力<rt>みりょく</rt></ruby>
Not only A but also B
<ruby>機能<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>だけでなく、デザインも<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>い
Not to mention A, even B
<ruby>基本<rt>きほん</rt></ruby>はおろか、<ruby>応用<rt>おうよう</rt></ruby>もできない

examples: He jumps to conclusions without even listening to what others say.
She criticized it without even reading the materials.
They came into the room without so much as a greeting.
Don't believe rumors without even looking into anything.
The kids don't even help out; they just play video games all the time.
They went out without even checking the time of the appointment.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker is annoyed and makes a negative evaluation of behavior that lacks the bare minimum.
Usually placed before a main clause that brings a bad consequence: ～もしないで＋(reaction/consequence).
Can be used for self-criticism:私は説明書を 読みもしないで 壊してしまった。
Natural in spoken language; in written language it can be replaced with ～もせずに to sound less harsh.

- Expresses “not doing V at all / not even bothering to do V (not even a little)” and then doing the next action. Implies reproach, criticism, annoyance.
- “も” means “even…” → combined with the negative “しない” it creates strong emphasis.
- Often used when talking about others, for behavior seen as lacking the bare minimum/common sense: “挨拶もしないで…”.
- Difference from ～ないで/～ずに (neutral): ～もしないで has an emotional nuance and emphasis.
fields.notes:
• “も” is placed right before “しない/せずに” or right after the noun of a する verb: 挨拶もしないで; 聞きもせずに.
• Putting “も” in the wrong place easily blurs the emphatic meaning: ×「も聞かないで」 (should be: 聞きもしないで).
• In polite language, the whole sentence can be shifted to です／ます, but the “～もしないで” part keeps its form.
mistakes: Wrong position of “も”: ×「聞くもしないで」 → correct: 「聞きもしないで」.
Confusing it with ～ないで/～ずに (which have no critical nuance). The JLPT often asks you to choose the pattern that expresses “not even bothering to…”.
Using it in a polite context with a superior can easily sound rude because of its reproachful nuance.
Forgetting to change to Vます: ×「行くもしないで」 → correct: 「行きもしないで」.

rows: <ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>まないで<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めた。
Close in meaning to ～もしないで, less emotional
<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>もせずに<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>った。
Does not connect to a following clause with “で”; reproachful nuance
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>なんて<ruby>聞<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きもしない。
Coarser, strongly expressive; does not mean “without doing… and then”

examples: If nothing is submitted by the deadline, it will be treated as a withdrawal.
We will reserve your seat on the understanding that payment of the participation fee has been confirmed.
The service is provided on the understanding that you have agreed to these Terms.
As you are regarded as a minor, parental consent is required.
An unexcused absence will be processed as a forfeiture.
fields.explain:
Formal; often appears in regulations, contracts, official notices, and business procedures.
Stiff nuance; establishes in advance a rule for handling situations that occur.
In everyday conversation, とみなす／として is more natural.

• Used to establish an assumption/convention: “regard as / be considered as / be treated as …”. Highly regulatory in nature.
• “Vた + ものとして” is very common: 合格したものとして手続きを進める（proceed with the procedures as if having passed）.
• “N + ものとして” is close to “N として” but emphasizes identification/definition within a framework of rules rather than a simple role.
fields.notes:
• Often follows a conditional clause: ～ない場合、…したものとして…. A set structure in regulations.
• “であるものとして” keeps the formal tone when attached to academic/legal nouns: 自然人であるものとして.
• In service notices, a polite variant: ～したものとして取り扱わせていただきます.
mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff: switch to とみなす／として when it is not a written document.
Confusing “Nとして” (role) with “Nであるものとして” (identification by convention): the legal meanings differ.
The JLPT often asks about the regulatory nuance and the form Vたものとして (regarded as having V-ed) in rule sentences.

rows: <ruby>欠席<rt>けっせき</rt></ruby>したものとして
Standard verb, easy to use in both spoken and written language; formal
Indicates only a role/function; no implied handling convention
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>として<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>
～<ruby>扱<rt>あつか</rt></ruby>い（として<ruby>扱<rt>あつか</rt></ruby>う）
Emphasizes the actual act of handling
<ruby>不在<rt>ふざい</rt></ruby><ruby>扱<rt>あつか</rt></ruby>いにする

examples: That one never shows up at the agreed time.
No matter how many times I explain, he just doesn't get it.
The kids never bother tidying up, yet all they do is complain.
Nobody's going to go to such an expensive place.
There's no way I can finish this much.
fields.explain:
Strong, coarse, leaning toward spoken language; avoid using it with superiors/in formal situations.
Often accompanied by evaluative words: どうせ／全然／まったく…＋Vやしない.
Used to refute expectations: 「頼んでも 来やしない よ」.
At the end of the sentence, nothing usually needs to be added after ～やしない.

- Emphasizes negation: “absolutely not / never ever / not even if it kills me…”. Expresses annoyance, sarcasm, criticism.
- Usually used in spoken language, with strong emotion. The subject is usually a person/target being criticized.
- Difference from ～もしないで: ～やしない does not have the sense “without doing… and then” to connect clauses; it only strongly negates the action.
fields.notes:
• “やしない” comes from “はしない” (a colloquial sound change). “りゃしない” is a contraction of “りはしない”.
• Combines widely with potential forms/forms of potential completion: 分かりゃしない／できやしない／終わりゃしない.
• In serious written language, prefer ～はしない or switch to another, more polite structure.
mistakes: Confusing its clause-connecting function: ～やしない is not used like ～ないで to connect “not doing A but doing B”.
Using it with superiors in formal writing → rude nuance.
Forgetting to change to Vます: ×「行くやしない」 → correct: 「行きやしない」.
Confusing it with ～っこない (possibility) in JLPT questions on nuance.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>りはしない。
Similar in meaning, but not as coarse as ～やしない
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きもしない。
No way / extremely unlikely to happen

<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>断<rt>ことわ</rt></ruby>るわけがない。

examples: Undaunted by the bad weather, he headed for the summit.
Undeterred by heavy criticism, she pushed ahead with the reforms.
Undeterred by illness, they carried on with their research.
Braving strong winds and high waves, the fishermen set sail.
Undaunted by the cold, the children are playing outside.
fields.explain:
Used to praise someone's spirit/determination; a narrative tone, describing heroism.
Avoid using it about yourself in humble contexts; if needed, soften the nuance: ～にもめげず／～に負けず.
Not used directly with clauses/verbs; it requires a noun denoting adversity.

• “In defiance of / think nothing of” – expresses an undaunted attitude in the face of adversity.
• Strong, literary nuance; used to give a high evaluation of the spirit of overcoming difficulties.
• Not applied to positive factors; combines only with negative/unfavorable agents.
fields.notes:
• Often accompanied by challenging vocabulary: 逆境、障害、重圧、痛み、非難、逆風.
• Useful in descriptive writing, encouraging speeches, and sports news.
• Usual word order: N（adversity）+ をものともせずに + V (toward a goal).
mistakes: Using it with positive factors (例: 応援をものともせず ×) → wrong scope of meaning.
Using it to praise yourself in a formal context → sounds boastful.
Confusing it with ～をよそに: the JLPT tests the nuance of praise vs. criticism.

rows: In defiance of, thinking nothing of
<ruby>困難<rt>こんなん</rt></ruby>をものともせず<ruby>挑<rt>いど</rt></ruby>む
Neutral; states a fact without implying praise
<ruby>大雨<rt>おおあめ</rt></ruby>にもかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>
～に<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けず／～にも<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けない

examples: Despite his parents' worries, he set off on a solo trip abroad.
Ignoring public criticism, the company continued to expand its business.
Ignoring the doctor's advice, he keeps on training excessively.
Disregarding their families' opposition, the two began living together.
Despite warnings of an approaching typhoon, some climbers went ahead and set out up the mountain.
Contrary to the expectations of those around her, she chose to start her own business rather than join a large company.
fields.explain:
Common nouns:親の心配・家族の反対・周囲の期待・世間の批判/非難・医者の忠告・危険/リスク・規則/ルール.
What follows: after ～をよそに comes a clause of intentional action (～する/～続ける/～強行する...).
Nuance of criticism/detachment: the speaker stands in the position of an observer who evaluates.
Strongly written in style; suits essays, newspapers, and news.

• In defiance of / ignoring / paying no heed to N: the person/group acts as if N (opposition, worry, expectations, warnings, public opinion...) did not exist.
• Evaluative nuance: implies criticism or surprise at “turning a deaf ear” to something that should have been heeded.
• Scope of use: mainly describes the actions of others/third parties; limit using it about yourself in formal contexts (used about yourself, it easily sounds like bragging about “defying everything”).
• Not used for spontaneous natural phenomena: it must be a volitional act. Avoid sentences like “天気をよそに雨が降った”.
• Formal/written; close in meaning to ～もかまわず but emphasizes “ignoring the reactions of those around” rather than “not minding the inconvenience”.
fields.notes:
• “よそ” originally means “elsewhere/outsider”, from which it came to mean “set aside, treat as unrelated”.
• In journalism, it often goes with 強行する・続行する・押し切る, creating a sense of criticism.
• When you want to praise the spirit of overcoming difficulties, choose ～をものともせず instead of ～をよそに to avoid a negative nuance.
mistakes: Used with natural phenomena: Incorrect. It must be a volitional act. × 雨をよそに降った → √ 雨にもかかわらず試合を行った。
Unsuitable N: Avoid neutral N such as 気温, 数字 unless they imply a “voice/warning”.
Using it about yourself in a formal context may be seen as self-aggrandizing; consider the point of view.
Confusing it with ～もかまわず: the latter emphasizes “not minding inconvenience”, not “ignoring other people's opinions”.

rows: Emphasizes “ignoring the voices around”; nuance of criticism.
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>の<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>をよそに<ruby>進学<rt>しんがく</rt></ruby>。
More neutral; the target is not necessarily “the voices around”.
<ruby>人目<rt>ひとめ</rt></ruby>もかまわず<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>く。
<ruby>困難<rt>こんなん</rt></ruby>をものともせず<ruby>挑戦<rt>ちょうせん</rt></ruby>する。
A structure linking clauses; no implication of “deliberately ignoring”.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>にもかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>。

examples: Because of heavy rain, the outdoor concert had to be canceled.
He was forced to retire due to illness.
Because of the pandemic, many schools were forced to switch to online classes.
Soaring raw material prices forced a review of the business plan.
Due to the earthquake, the second-round exam had to be postponed.
Sluggish demand forced job cuts.
fields.explain:
The passive subject is the party that “has to accept” it (人/組織/イベント…), not the cause.
The cause (natural disasters, epidemics, the market…) usually becomes the subject in the active form ～を余儀なくする.
Not used for trivial everyday matters; preferred for decisions/scales of a social/official nature.
Stiff, objective nuance; avoid using it when you want to assign blame subjectively.

• “Be forced to / have no choice but N”: expresses reluctance due to circumstances/objective pressure.
• N must be a noun that can form a サ変 verb (an act/measure): 中止・延期・変更・撤退・縮小・移行・辞任・閉鎖・解散・見直し…
• Often preceded by a cause phrase with により・ため・せいで.
• Literary nuance; often used in news, reports, and press releases.
fields.notes:
• “余儀ない” = “there is no other way”. This structure is fixed; avoid altering it arbitrarily.
• Avoid overusing it with N that is not an act (× 景気を余儀なくされる); change it to a related act (縮小・撤退 etc.).
• In administrative writing, combine it with により/に伴い/の影響で to state an objective cause.
mistakes: Attaching it directly to a verb: Incorrect. × 行くを余儀なくされる → √ 出席を余儀なくされる.
Confusing the subject: the “party that is forced” is the subject of ～を余儀なくされる.
Confusing it with せざるを得ない: that one goes with verbs and has a personal nuance; exams often ask you to distinguish the type of word it attaches to.
Using it in small personal contexts (shopping, errands) sounds too formal and unnatural.

examples: This plan is being carried out on the premise that everyone will participate.
The contract is concluded on the premise that the relationship of trust will continue.
The model was evaluated on the premise that the data were accurate.
A schedule that presupposes securing a sufficient budget is not realistic.
On the premise that third-party consent is obtained, the release will take place next month.
fields.explain:
Common combinations:参加・合意・継続・確保・存在・達成・安定・正常稼働など + を前提として.
Used to state policy/design assumptions; state them clearly to avoid misunderstanding the scope of application.
Compared with ～を前提にして, ～を前提として is more formal, leaning toward statements of principles/definitions.

• Establishes a “premise/something taken for granted as true” in order to proceed with a plan, discussion, or design.
• Unlike a condition “if… then…”, 前提 is a foundational assumption: one proceeds as if it were already true.
• Often used in policy, business, academic, and technical contexts; formal nuance.
• When the premise is off, the conclusion/design may become invalid; therefore it often goes with verification/見直し.
fields.notes:
• If you want to emphasize that “the assumption may change”, add a word meaning temporary: 当面/暫定的に + ～を前提として.
• In research, it is often accompanied by a scope condition: 本研究はXの環境を前提として評価を行う。
• To avoid ambiguity, when the premise is a long clause, prefer という前提で.
mistakes: Confusing it with the condition “if… then…”. 前提 is something taken for granted that already exists, not a future condition.
Attaching a long clause directly to を前提として makes the sentence heavy; という前提で is more natural.
Confusing it with ～を前提にして when choosing the nuance; exams often test your feel for formality/implementation.

rows: Used in documents and normative statements.
<ruby>全員<rt>ぜんいん</rt></ruby><ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>として
Leans toward operation/practice; natural in on-site settings.
スマホ<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>にして
Does not imply “assumed true” but “a source of reference”.
データに<ruby>基<rt>もと</rt></ruby>づいて<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>
More natural when the subject is a clause.
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>するという<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>で
